questions.stem: A 45-year-old man presented with a 2-day history of rash and fever. He had returned 1 week before his symptoms began from a 4-week holiday in Nigeria visiting family. He worked as a postal worker. On examination his temperature was 38.7°C, his heart rate was 110 beats/minute, and his blood pressure was 110/64 mmHg. He had a vesicular rash affecting predominantly his trunk, with many vesicles that were easy to burst. There are some macular lesions as well as the vesicles.
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Chickenpox The characteristic rash, with vesicles affecting the trunk as opposed to extremities, and easy to slough off, indicates chickenpox as the likely diagnosis. He could have been exposed to monkeypox in Nigeria as there are ongoing outbreaks, but the rash in monkeypox largely affects the face and extremities. He is also a postal worker, an occupational risk factor for exposure to bioterrorist acts, but the rash distribution, and the lesions at differing stages of development are against a diagnosis such as smallpox.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 1 Q46

questions.stem: A 54-year-old pet store owner presented with 4 days of fever and headache, and 2 days of a rash that had started on his face and spread outward. On examination, he had a macular rash over his face and distal extremities, with only a few lesions on his abdomen and back. His temperature was 38.3°C. He had widespread lymphadenopathy. Examination of his cardiovascular, respiratory, and abdominal examinations was unremarkable. He was admitted for observation and investigation. Over the next few days the rash evolved from macules to vesicles to pustules. The fever persisted for 8 days in total, the rash for 12 days. Electron microscopy of lesion biopsy:
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely pathogen?
questions.explanation: Intrauterine death The diagnosis of monkeypox infection requires clinical (rash), epidemiologic (equatorial Africa), and laboratory (the presence of genomic DNA or brick-shaped virions in scab material) findings. parts.text: List 1 infection (causative organism not required) under each category that cause an eschar - Rickettsial

cohort_answer.text: Rickettsial: Scrub typhus, murine typhus, epidemic typhus, african tick bite fever (Orientia tsutsugamushi, rickettsia africae). Bacterial (non-rickettsial): Tularemia, plague (Francisella tularensis, yersinia pestis); Ecthyma (pseudomonas). Virus: Smallpox, vaccinia

parts.text: Which antiviral is health Canada approved for Mpox

questions.model_answer: Tecovirimat (TPOXX) is the antiviral approved by Health Canada for mpox.
questions.beyond_mandell: Health Canada authorization for tecovirimat (mpox indication).

parts.text: Remdesivir treatment efficacy as per animal models

cohort_answer.text:
3 proteins: Envelope; Membrane; Nucleocapsid.
Approved treatment for Mpox: Tecovirimat (Tpoxx) - potent inhibitor of an orthopoxvirus protein required for formation of an infectious virus particle, essential for dissemination within an infected host. (Cidofovir has in vitro activity against monkeypox virus and shown effective against lethal monkeypox virus challenge in animal models.)
Remdesivir efficacy in animal models: In a study of 12 macaques, 6 treated with Remdesivir and 6 not; of the 6 treated only 1 developed dyspnea vs all of the untreated. Outpatient treatment: 4/246 (1.6%) treated arm vs 21/252 (8.3%) placebo arm required a medical visit. Inpatient treatment: 1062 randomized to remdesivir or placebo; median recovery time 10 days vs 15 days; mortality at day 15: 6.7% vs 11.9%; mortality at day 29: 11.4% vs 15.2%.

questions.question: A 24 year old man who had sex with multiple men presents with this rash: [image-based question: rash in an MSM patient]

parts.text: What is ONE off-label treatment for this condition?
What is the gene target or viral protein target of this treatment?

questions.model_answer:
a) Diagnosis: mpox (monkeypox).
b) Off-label treatment: tecovirimat.
c) Target: the viral p37 envelope-wrapping protein (VP37, encoded by the F13L homolog), which tecovirimat inhibits, blocking formation of the enveloped virion and viral egress/cell-to-cell spread.
